attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, game directions, sprite set up, Player sprite overlaps Enemy sprite, Player sprite overlaps Food sprite.


Start each comment with //﻿ and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite to move with direction buttons and stay in screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the default sprite kind used in the Player sprite code? What other sprite kinds might be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that just like in the blocks editor, the default sprite kind parameter is set to Player. In this level, the ninja will customize sprite kinds to create unique overlap events.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // sprite set up. Select a Player sprite from the gallery or My Assets and update the sprite name. Notice the default sprite kind argument is set to SpriteKind.Player.


Move the Player sprite with direction buttons. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the Player sprite code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. 


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the movement code. Update the Player sprite’s name, and use the default argument true.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the sprite kind for each sprite in the sprite.create function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is changing a sprite kind in the JavaScript editor, similar and different to the blocks editor?

❓ Which sprite kinds are available in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Emphasize the connection between changing sprite kinds in the JavaScript and blocks editor. In blocks, the ninja was able to select a new sprite kind from an embedded drop-down menu within the block and it was easy to add new sprite kinds. In the JavaScript editor, a dot operator can be used to access the same list of sprite kinds, which contains: Player, Projectile, Food, and Enemy.
steps.instructions:
Add Food and Enemy sprites to the project.


Create a Food sprite by opening Sprites and dragging [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the Player sprite code under // sprite set up. Select an image from the gallery or My Assets and update the sprite name. 


Just as in the blocks editor, sprite kinds can be changed in the JavaScript editor. Change the kind parameter by deleting .Player. Retype the dot operator . then notice the 4 sprite kinds that appear in the code completion tool. Select Food from the list of properties .



Create an Enemy sprite by opening Sprites again and dragging [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the code that sets the Food sprite. Update the sprite name and image, then change the kind parameter to SpriteKind.Enemy


Click ▶ to see a Food and Enemy sprite appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the sprite’s x and y-coordinates to be randomly selected from a range of values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the Food and Enemy sprites be placed on the screen?

❓ Did you update the sprite name in the Enemy sprite’s position code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that using 10 in the randint ranges can prevent the sprite from appearing too close to the edges of the screen.
steps.instructions:
Place the Food and Enemy sprites randomly on the screen!


Set the Food sprite’s position by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the Food sprite. 

Use randint to set the sprite’s x-position between 10 and screen.width - 10 and to set the y-position between 10 and screen.height - 10


Copy (Ctrl + C) the Food sprite’s position code and paste (Ctrl + V) it underneath the code that sets the Enemy sprite. Update the code with the Enemy sprite’s name. 


Click ▶ to see both the Food and Enemy sprites appear in random positions on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the onUpdateInterval loop to move Enemy sprites to random positions at a set time interval?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is setting a sprite’s lifespan in the JavaScript editor similar and different to the blocks editor?

❓ What might the minimum and maximum possible values be for the Enemy sprite’s lifespan?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the blocks editor, the ninja used the [set sprite [x]] block to select the set a sprite’s lifespan in milliseconds. This block could also be used to set a variety of sprite properties. Similarly, in the JavaScript editor, a sprite’s properties can be accessed through the dot operator. After selecting lifespan, the ninja can use an assignment operator and a number value, to set how long the sprite will stay on the screen.

💡 Remind the ninja to consider how frequently Enemy sprites appear on screen, when setting the range of lifespan values.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprite to appear at a set interval, then randomize how long it stays on the screen!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] underneath the Enemy sprite’s code. Cut (Ctrl + X) the Enemy sprite’s code and and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop. Tinker with the parameter to set how often an Enemy sprite will appear on the screen. 


Underneath the Enemy sprite’s position code, type the Enemy sprite’s name followed by a dot operator .


Scroll down to the properties in the code completion tool and select lifespan.



Then, type an assignment operator = and use randint to set a range, in milliseconds, of possible values for the Enemy sprite’s lifespan to be set to.

 

Click ▶ to see Enemy sprites appear on screen at a regular interval, then disappear after a random amount of time.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to Player and otherKind parameter to Enemy in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is creating an overlap event in the JavaScript editor similar and different to the blocks editor?

❓ What might happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that in the blocks editor, they used an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container to create an overlap event. In the container, the sprite was able to set the kind and otherKind parameters via drop-down menus, then place code to run on sprite overlap inside of the container. In the JavaScript editor, the kind and otherKind parameters are set using the dot operator, and the code that runs on sprite overlap is located inside the event’s curly brackets { }.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite!

 

Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // Player sprite overlaps Enemy sprite. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.onOverlap(SpriteKind.Player, SpriteKind.Player, function(sprite: Sprite, otherSprite: Sprite) { })

The onOverlap event takes 3 parameters: kind, otherKind, and handler. The kind parameter sets the first type of sprite to check for, the otherKind parameter sets the second type of sprite to check for, and the handler parameter sets the code to run when the 2 sprite kinds overlap.


Leave the default kind parameter set to SpriteKind.Player. Update the otherKind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . then selecting Enemy from the list of properties .

 

Now, the project will check if a Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, and will run code inside the curly brackets { } if true.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the sprite name in the sprites.destroy(mySprite) code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is otherSprite used in the destroy code?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that otherSprite refers to the sprite kind used in the otherKind parameter: SpriteKind.Enemy. Rather than using a specific sprite, the code looks for any instance of an Enemy sprite overlapping a Player sprite. On overlap, the Enemy sprite is destroyed.
steps.instructions:
Destroy the Enemy sprite on overlap with the Player sprite!

 

Open Sprites and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.destroy(mySprite)

To ensure that any Enemy sprite is destroyed on overlap with the Player sprite, replace mySprite with otherSprite inside the parentheses.

 

Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the value parameters for both info.setLife and changeLifeBy?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using a life variable in the JavaScript editor similar and different than the blocks editor?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 With the reintroduction of the life variable, the ninja will have another tool to customize projects in JavaScript. The setLife and changeLifeBy functions operate very similarly in both editors. Both functions take 1 value to set either the number of lives that the sprite begins with or the value that the number of lives changes by, when a specific event occurs.

💡 Walk through the logic of the onOverlap event with the ninja. When the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, the Enemy sprite will be destroyed and the number of lives will decrease by 1.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to lose a life on overlap with an Enemy sprite!

 

Open Info and drag [set life to (3)] underneath // set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.setLife(3)

The setLife function takes 1 parameter: value, or the number of lives. Tinker with the value parameter to set how many lives the Player sprite will start with at the beginning of the project.

 

Open Info and drag [change life by (-1)] underneath the destroy code inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.changeLifeBy(-1)

The changeLifeBy function takes 1 parameter: value, or the number of lives that will be changed. Keep the default argument set to -1.

 

Click ▶ to see the Player sprite lose a life when it overlaps with an Enemy sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to Player and otherKind parameter to Food in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does it matter which sprite kind is used as the kind parameter and which is used as the otherKind parameter in an onOverlap event?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 At this point in JavaScript, the ninja has used overlap code to check if a single sprite has overlapped with another single sprite. In that case, it did not matter which sprite was used in each parameter. When using an onOverlap event, the order of each sprite kind does not necessarily matter, however the handler function parameter (sprite or otherSprite) used should match the corresponding sprite kind.

💡 Walk through the logic of the onOverlap event with the ninja. When the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite, the Food sprite will move to a random position on screen.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite!

 

Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // Player sprite overlaps Food sprite.


Leave the default kind parameter set to SpriteKind.Player Update the otherKind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . then selecting Food from the list of properties .

 

Copy (Ctrl + C) the Food sprite’s position code and and paste (Ctrl + V) it on a blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Replace the Food sprite’s name by typing otherSprite.

 

Click ▶ to see the Food sprite’s position change when the Player sprite overlaps it!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add changeScoreBy inside the curly brackets { } of the Player and Food sprite onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite?

❓ Why is otherSprite not used in the changeScoreBy code?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the logic of the onOverlap event with the ninja. When the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite, the Food sprite will move to a random position on screen and the score will increase by 1.

💡Point out to the ninja that the handler parameter (otherSprite) only needs to be used when the code is changing a specific sprite property or action. Because the changeScoreBy function is not attached to a specific sprite, otherSprite does not need to be used.
steps.instructions:
Score a point when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite!

 

Open Info and drag [set score to (value)] underneath // set up Leave the default argument set to 0.

 

Open Info again and drag [change score by (1)] inside the curly brackets { } of the Player/Food sprite onOverlap event, underneath the Food sprite’s position code. Tinker with the score value to set how many points the Player sprite will earn on overlap with the Food sprite.

 

Click ▶ to see the Player sprite score points on overlap with a Food sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an equality operator == to check if the score is equal to a certain number of points?
steps.instructions:
End the game when the Player sprite has earned a certain number of points!

 

Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the Player/Food sprite onOverlap event, underneath the existing code. Replace true by opening Info and dragging [score] inside the parentheses. Type an equality operator == and a goal value for the Player sprite to reach.

 

Open Game and drag [game over (true)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition. Keep the default argument set to true. Add an optional screen effect, too.

 

Click ▶ to see the game end in a win once the Player sprite has earned a certain number of points!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help players understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game?

❓ What sounds might be played when each onOverlap event occurs?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color, directions, and sound effects!

 

Open Scene and drag [set background color to (color)] underneath // set up. Set a color parameter using a number 1-15.

 

Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath // game directions. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.

 

Open Music and drag [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] underneath the changeLifeBy and changeScoreBy code in the different onOverlap events. Use the dot operator . to select a sound from the code completion tool.

 

Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses sprite overlap events to make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps with different sprite kinds.

validationItems.text: Use 1 Player sprite with a custom name, move it with the controller, and keep it in the screen.
Use 1 Food sprite with a custom name. Give it a random starting position.
Create an Enemy sprite inside an onUpdateInterval loop. Randomize its position and lifespan.
When the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, destroy the Enemy sprite and decrease the lives count.
When the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite, change the Food sprite’s position and increase the score.
End the game when the player’s score reaches 10.
Change the background color, use long text to give the player instructions, and add sound effects.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about sprite kinds and sprite overlap events. In the JavaScript editor, you can use a namespace to create new sprite kinds. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: One of a Kind
badges.description: Use sprite kinds and events to control what happens to sprites in a project in JavaScript.

badges.title: A Meeting of the Kinds
badges.description: Use an overlap event that runs based on the sprites’ kinds.

badges.title: Nice Knowing Ya
badges.description: Write code that destroys a sprite.

badges.title: Life of the Party
badges.description: Set the value of the Player’s life.

badges.title: From One Sprite to Another
badges.description: Create a projectile that starts from the position of an existing sprite.

badges.title: Metamorphosis
badges.description: Change the sprite kind of an existing sprite.

badges.title: Kind of You to Join
badges.description: Create a new sprite kind in JavaScript.

badges.title: New Kind on the Block
badges.description: Write code that runs when a sprite with a specific sprite kind is created.

badges.title: Out of Chances
badges.description: Write code that runs when the Player’s life reaches zero.

badges.title: Spice Up Your Life
badges.description: Set the image used to represent the Player’s life.
